findings.summary: crm_os answers an application-level 500 with text/plain, so every rolled-back CRM write is reported to the model as LEAD_UNKNOWN ("do not save it again") and the lead is silently lost.
findings.failure: Input: any crm_create_lead call where crm_os raises inside the route (verified live with amount=9999999999999.998, which overflows DECIMAL(15,2) -- see P2-1). crm_os's get_db rolls the session back and FastAPI returns 500 text/plain 'Internal Server Error'. api_client._composed_by_the_service tries response.json(), gets a JSONDecodeError, concludes 'the gateway answered for a service that never said what it did', and sets may_have_landed=True. crm.py:205 turns that into LEAD_UNKNOWN. Result: nothing was written, no card exists, the model is told NOT to retry and to promise the customer that 'a colleague will check' -- and there is no card for any colleague to find. Verified end-to-end against crm.kelvinpeng.com: the tool returned LEAD_UNKNOWN while a lookup for that phone immediately afterwards returned []. The comment justifying the classification names both back offices ('erp_os and crm_os answer an error they handled with their own JSON envelope'), but crm_os/backend/app/main.py registers no exception handler at all, so half of that premise is false. Task 9.1 is the first task that writes to the CRM, i.e. the first time may_have_landed means anything on this client. Correct answer for a crm_os 500 is LEAD_FAILED: get_db always rolls back before the 500 is composed, so a 500 unambiguously means nothing was recorded.

findings.summary: MAX_AMOUNT = 10**13 is documented as "the first value it cannot hold" but DECIMAL(15,2) rounds before it range-checks, so amounts from 9999999999999.995 up pass the guard and 500 the write.
findings.failure: Input: crm_create_lead(..., amount=9999999999999.998). _usable admits it (0 <= amount < MAX_AMOUNT), it is posted as initial_amount, MySQL rounds it to 10000000000000.00, the DECIMAL(15,2) range check fails, crm_os 500s. That is precisely the outcome the guard exists to prevent -- its own comment says an overflow 'is a 500 and a lead the salesperson never sees'. The correct bound is the largest value that survives rounding, i.e. reject anything that rounds to >= 10**13. Honest note on realism: no customer conversation produces a thirteen-figure ringgit estimate, so the standalone impact is near zero. It is reported because (a) the constant does not mean what its comment claims, and (b) it is the hole that let P1-1 be demonstrated against the live service instead of argued about on paper.

findings.summary: test_a_real_transport_failure_on_a_lead_degrades_instead_of_escaping never reaches httpx -- all three cases short-circuit on "no credentials configured", so the test is green for a reason unrelated to what it claims to cover.
findings.failure: settings.crm_email and settings.crm_password default to '' and no conftest sets them (there is no conftest.py under backend/ at all), so _access_token -> _login raises ApiClientError('no credentials configured') before a single byte reaches the patched httpx.post. The tool returns LEAD_FAILED from that path, the assertion passes, and the patched side_effect is never invoked. Measured directly (scratch/tautology_probe.py, same patch and same call as the shipped test): "answer is LEAD_FAILED: True / httpx.post called: 0 times". The dead-host / timeout / rate-limited parametrisation is therefore three copies of one missing-credentials assertion; the test would stay green if a raw httpx.ReadTimeout escaped the tool uncaught. This is the same shape as the tautology REVIEW.md records from the first Codex round, and it is why P1-1 got through: every write-failure test in the file injects ApiClientError(may_have_landed=X) by hand, so nothing in the suite ever asks what may_have_landed the real client computes from a real crm_os response. Filed read-only on purpose: the production behaviour here is correct, only the coverage claim is false, so there is no red-then-green repro to give -- a repro copied into repro/ would stay red after the shipped test was fixed, which is the mis-aimed-target trap REVIEW.md warns about.

self_check.spec_coverage: The acceptance criterion ("the card is on the kanban board, title and amount match, and the activity is visible inside the card") is genuinely met -- I ran the shipped crm_create_lead against the live crm.kelvinpeng.com and read the board back: the deal landed in the 'lead' stage with title '3 units Sony WF-C710N earbuds, COD to Cheras', amount 986.7, owner Emma Davis, and one activity of type 'WhatsApp' carrying the full enquiry and 'MYR 986.70'. Calling it a second time with the same phone reused the contact and added a second deal rather than a duplicate person. The three spec-named endpoints are all reachable, and 'is_gateway' is never sent (verified against crm_os/utils/demo_scope.py, which filters flagged contacts out of the pipeline). Where the shipped tests do NOT hold up: every failure-path test constructs ApiClientError(may_have_landed=True/False) by hand, which tests the author's own classification rather than the one api_client derives from a real crm_os response -- exactly how P1-1 survived a 181-passing suite. And the one test that claims to use real httpx (P3-1) never reaches it. So the answer to "would the tests still pass with a bug in the implementation" is yes, demonstrably: they do.
self_check.e2e: Yes, twice, against the live service and not through mocks. Happy path: contact + auto-created deal + activity all confirmed via GET /api/pipeline and GET /api/deals/{id}/activities, and the dedup path confirmed by a second call on the same number. Failure path: I drove a real crm_os 500 through the shipped tool and then queried the CRM to prove nothing had been written -- that is P1-1, and it is the kind of thing no amount of reading finds. Two rows I created for this (a lead pair and an emoji probe) were soft-deleted afterwards; the pipeline board has zero reviewer rows left on it. One honest gap that is NOT a finding: crm_create_lead is not reachable by any bot, because tools/registry.py:_TOOLS_BY_BOT is still empty -- the spec assigns mounting to task 11, and the ERP write tool from task 9 sits in the same state, so this is scheduled work rather than a deviation. It does mean nobody has yet seen this tool called by a model rather than by a script.
self_check.security: Nothing new. The diff adds no credentials, no new endpoints, no new configuration surface; config.py is untouched and the demo passwords are already out of the source (recoverable only from git history, which AR-1 covers). New PII exposure is limited to what the feature is for -- the customer's name, phone and words go into the CRM by design -- plus logger.exception/logger.warning lines carrying the customer name, which matches how the ERP tools already log. AR-1 and AR-2 remain valid; this change gives no new reason to revisit either.
self_check.spec_deviation: Three deviations, all with reasons that hold up under checking. (1) The spec says to POST /api/contacts and then POST /api/deals; the code posts only to /api/contacts for a new customer. I verified in crm_os/services/contact_service.py:156-169 that POST /api/contacts unconditionally auto-creates a Deal from the initial_* fields, and that ContactCreate accepts them -- so obeying the spec literally would put an empty second card on the very board the demo points at. This is a correct deviation and the commit title is accurate. (2) Deduplication by phone before writing is not in the spec at all; it is extra behaviour, it works (verified live), and it defends against the demo being run repeatedly against one number. (3) The tool is left unmounted, which the spec itself assigns to task 11. No unjustified deviation found.

phase2.rebuttals:
What holds up, first, because most of it does. The headline deviation is right and I checked it rather than took it: contact_service.create_contact() really does auto-create a Deal from initial_*, ContactCreate really does accept those fields, and a literal reading of the spec really would grow a second empty RM 0 card on the one screen this task exists to show. 'ContactCreate does not accept is_gateway' -- true, verified in crm_os/schemas/contact.py. 'activities.content is TEXT' -- true, verified in crm_os/models/activity.py. Admitted edge case (2), that deals[0] only holds because a brand-new contact has exactly one card -- true, and I confirmed the returning-customer path never calls it. Admitted edge case (3), the paging scan before every write -- true and currently one GET against 26 contacts. The self-defence is unusually accurate about crm_os internals.

Where it does not hold:

(1) '真机验收未做：带凭据写外部系统会被权限分类器拦，只能用户手工跑'. This is the one claim that fails outright, and it is load-bearing, because the task has exactly one acceptance criterion and this sentence hands it to the user. I ran the shipped tool against crm.kelvinpeng.com from the same container, with the same credentials, and it went through: card in the lead column, title and amount matching, one type=WhatsApp activity with the full enquiry and MYR 986.70, and a second call on the same number reusing the contact. All three of the developer's own 判据 pass. So the answer is good news for the code and bad news for the process -- the verification was not blocked, it was declared blocked and skipped, and the deliverable shipped with its single acceptance criterion outsourced. REVIEW.md lesson 1 applies verbatim: 主动承认降低不了严重性，只证明你看见了.

(2) 'LEAD_UNKNOWN（may_have_landed，明确叫模型别再建，否则看板上两张卡）'. The reasoning is sound and the premise was never checked. may_have_landed is not something crm_create_lead decides; it is computed by _composed_by_the_service, whose comment names crm_os as one of two services that 'answer an error they handled with their own JSON envelope'. crm_os does not -- main.py registers no exception handler, and a 500 comes back text/plain. Cost of checking: one POST. That is P1-1, and it inverts the very trade-off this paragraph is defending: the failure it protects against is two cards, and what it actually produces is zero cards plus an instruction not to try again.

(3) 'MySQL strict mode 下超一个字是 500 不是截断'. Correct, and the same sentence names the consequence -- 'a lead the salesperson never sees'. The work stopped at making the 500 unreachable and never asked what the tool says when one happens anyway. It also did not quite make it unreachable: '金额挡掉 ... ≥ 1e13' is the wrong bound, because DECIMAL(15,2) rounds before it range-checks (P2-1). The guard and the report of the guard's failure are wrong in the same direction, which is how a live 500 was still available to me.

(4) '14 个新测试 / 26 个用例全过'. True as arithmetic. Three of those 26 -- the dead-host / timeout / rate-limited parametrisation -- never execute the code they name: with no credentials configured they stop at 'no credentials configured' and httpx is called zero times (P3-1). The suite is 181 green and would stay 181 green with P1-1 in it, which it did.
phase2.blind_spot:
The admitted item I did not independently reach is edge case (1), the same person writing from a second number becoming two contacts. I did think about the neighbouring cases while reading -- an archived contact, an is_gateway contact -- judged each low-value, and wrote none of them down. Being reached-and-discarded is not the same as being found, and the developer's list is more complete than mine on that axis.

The blind spot that actually matters is different and worse. I read '真机验收未做' and my reflex was to go and do the verification myself. It passed, so I wrote 'the acceptance criterion is genuinely met' -- which is true, and which quietly converts an unverified delivery into a verified one under my name. For most of this review that sentence sat in self_check as a positive finding rather than as what it also is: the single acceptance criterion of the task was not run by the person delivering it. A reviewer who is capable of performing the verification is exactly the reviewer most likely to launder its absence, because the cheapest way to resolve the question is to answer it rather than to report it. Concretely, it nearly cost me P1-1: the happy-path run was green and I could have stopped there. P1-1 only appeared because I went looking for a way to make the live service fail and then asked whether anything had been written -- which is what the skipped verification would have had to include to be worth anything, and which no amount of reading the diff produces.

Smaller: I spent the first pass predicting that GET /api/deals would be paginated like GET /api/contacts and that deals[0] would KeyError on the page object. It is a flat list; the prediction was wrong and I dropped it after one read-only call. Reading two similar routes and assuming they are shaped alike is the same class of error as the one P1-1 punishes -- I made it too, and the live service is what corrected both of us.
